cues.text:
A man in a business suit
hijacked a passenger jet,
collected two hundred thousand dollars,
and parachuted into a freezing night.

More than fifty years later, the FBI
still cannot tell you his name.

Almost every crime
leaves something behind.
A fingerprint on a glass.
A body in the ground.
A name, a face, a witness, a paper

trail that, with enough time and
enough people pulling on it,
eventually leads somewhere.
This one led nowhere.
On the night before Thanksgiving,

in 1971, a quiet man talked
his way onto a passenger plane,

threatened it with a bomb,
collected a fortune in cash,

and walked out the back of the
aircraft into the dark sky.
He was never seen again.

Not his face, not his body, not
the money strapped to his chest.

He simply stopped existing somewhere over
the forests of the Pacific Northwest,
and he has stayed gone ever since.

The world came to know him by
a name that was never even his.

D.B. Cooper. Over the next fifty years
that name grew into something far stranger
than a criminal.

It became a legend, an unsolved itch
the country could not stop scratching.
More than eight hundred suspects.
A forty-five-year manhunt.

Books, songs, conventions, and a single
bundle of rotting twenty-dollar bills dug
out of a riverbank by a child.

None of it was ever
enough to give him a name.
It helps to know the moment he stepped

into. The early 1970s were the golden
age of the airplane hijacking in America.

There were dozens of
them, year after year,

so many that flight crews were
quietly trained to go along with it,

to keep everyone calm,
hand over what was asked,

and get the plane safely
back on the ground.

Most of those hijackers
wanted a destination,

usually Cuba, and a cause
they could shout about.
This man wanted none of that.
No country, no manifesto, no audience.
He wanted cash, and a parachute,
and a way to walk off the edge of the map.

That alone set him apart before
he had done anything at all.

Over the next half hour we
are going to do three things.

First, we will walk through exactly
what happened that night,

minute by minute, because the calm of
it is somehow more chilling than any
violence would have been.

Then we will look at the only solid
piece of evidence the case ever produced,
and what it does and does not prove.

And finally we will sit with the
question that has outlived nearly

everyone who ever chased it. Who was
he, and did he even survive the fall?

After half a century, the honest answer
is also the most maddening one there is.
Nobody knows.

He bought his ticket under
the name Dan Cooper.
A short hop, Portland to Seattle,

the kind of late-afternoon flight
nobody is supposed to remember.
He paid cash. He carried a briefcase.

He took a seat near the
back of the Boeing 727,
ordered a drink, and waited.
By the descriptions that survive,

he looked like a middle-aged
businessman in a dark suit and a thin tie.
Forgettable, almost certainly on purpose.
The famous initials came later,
and by accident.
In the chaos of that first night,
a wire-service report garbled the details,

and the wrong name went
out across the country.

It stuck. The man on the plane
called himself Dan Cooper.
The world has called him D.B.

Cooper ever since, which means
that even his fake name is,

in a small way, a mistake
nobody ever managed to correct.

Not long after takeoff, he handed
a note to one of the flight attendants.

She was young, working
the back of the cabin,

and her first instinct was to assume it
was a lonely businessman slipping her his

phone number. She tucked the paper
into her pocket without reading it.
He leaned toward her, calm and quiet,
and told her she had better take a look.
The note said he had a bomb.

He opened the briefcase just
enough for her to see inside.
A nest of wires.

Rows of red cylinders that looked
exactly like sticks of dynamite.

Whether any of it was real, nobody
on that airplane could possibly know,
and that uncertainty was the whole weapon.

A bomb you cannot test
is a bomb that works.
Then he told her what he wanted,

and the precision of the list is the first
sign that this was not improvised.

Two hundred thousand
dollars, in twenty-dollar bills.
And four parachutes.
Two main chutes, two reserves.

Investigators have turned that parachute
detail over for fifty years.
Four chutes, for one man.

Why four? The leading idea is
chilling in its cleverness.

By asking for four, he made
the authorities believe he might

force one of the crew or
passengers to jump alongside him.

And if an innocent person
might be going out that door,
the parachutes could not be rigged,

could not be sabotaged,
could not be packed to fail.

He had quietly guaranteed
himself working equipment,
without ever saying so.
That is not panic.
That is planning.

What unsettles everyone
who studies that flight,
though, is not the threat.
It is the manner of the man making it.
He was unfailingly polite the entire time.
He lit a cigarette.

He ordered a bourbon and
soda and drank it slowly.

While the crew quietly understood
that the airplane was now his,

the man at the center of it
behaved like a passenger

mildly inconvenienced by
a delayed connection.
No shouting. No sweating.

Just a calm, courteous
stranger who happened to be

holding a planeload of people
in the palm of his hand.

The plane circled near
Seattle while the money

and the parachutes were gathered
on the ground, then landed.

There the exchange
happened, fast and tense.

The cash and the chutes
were carried aboard.

In return, he kept his
word and let the passengers go.

About thirty-six of them
filed off the plane,
most of them never quite realizing,
until they read about it later,

how close they had been to the most
famous skyjacking in American history.
He kept only a small crew.

The two pilots up front,
a flight engineer,
and one flight attendant.

Then the plane was refueled
for the next, stranger leg.
None of this happened in a rush,

and the patience of it is
part of what unnerves people.

While the airline scrambled on the ground
to gather two hundred thousand dollars
in twenties and round up four parachutes,
the plane stayed in the air near Seattle,

circling, burning fuel, for
the better part of two hours.

Two full hours of a calm man in a
window seat with a lit cigarette,
and a cabin of passengers

who, for the most part, still had no
idea that anything at all was wrong.

The flight attendant seated closest to him
spent much of that time at his side,

carrying his demands to
the cockpit and back.

By her account he was
not a snarling villain.
He was composed, almost courteous,

the particular kind of polite that is
somehow more frightening than shouting,

because it tells you the man has thought
all of this through and is in no hurry
whatsoever.
Picture the ransom itself for a second.

Two hundred thousand
dollars, all in twenties,
is around ten thousand separate bills,

and it weighs something
close to twenty pounds.
He had it brought aboard in a bag,
and by the accounts that survive,

he lashed that bag to his
body before he jumped.
A grown man in a business suit,

about to step into a freezing
storm at two hundred miles an hour,

with a twenty-pound brick of
cash strapped to his chest.

His instructions to the cockpit were
unusual enough that the pilots had to push
back on some of them.
Fly toward Mexico City.
Stay low, under ten thousand feet.

Keep the speed down,
the wing flaps lowered,
the landing gear hanging in the wind.

And leave the rear staircase,
the aft airstair, unlocked.

Notice what those demands
quietly revealed about him.

This was not a man who had wandered
onto just any flight with a vague

idea and a fake bomb. He had
chosen a Boeing 727 on purpose,

and he understood its one unusual feature
better than most passengers ever would.

He knew it could be flown slow and
low with the rear stairs down.

He knew a person could drop straight out
of the back of it into open air and clear
the aircraft cleanly.
Whoever he was, he knew airplanes,

and he had picked the exact
machine that turned
an impossible escape into a workable plan.

You have to understand
the machine he had chosen.

The Boeing 727 carried a set of
stairs built into its tail,
under the fuselage.

On the ground, passengers could
walk down them onto the tarmac.

In the air, with the right
plane and the right nerve,

they could be lowered
straight into open sky.

Up in the locked cockpit, the crew
watched a small warning light tell

them that the back of their own
airplane had just opened to the night.

What happened next is the entire reason
we are still talking about this man.

Somewhere over the dark, wooded
country of southwestern Washington,
a little after eight in the evening,
he made his way to the back of the cabin.

He went down those open stairs into a
roaring wall of freezing air and rain,

the plane moving near two
hundred miles an hour,
the cash strapped to his body.
And he stepped off.
The crew felt him go.
A subtle shift in the airplane's balance,
a small bump as a weight left the tail.

They called to him over the
intercom and got nothing back.

He was already falling through the night
toward a forest he could not see,

in conditions that would
have frightened a trained

paratrooper with a map
and a moonlit drop zone.
He had neither.
Hold on the cold for a moment,

because the cold is
the heart of the gamble.

He went out the back of that jet in a
business suit and a thin trench coat,

into air far below freezing,
into driving rain and darkness,
over steep, timbered terrain, at night,

with no lights below to aim for and
no way to know whether he was

about to land in a clearing or in
the top of a hundred-foot tree.

Experienced skydivers turn down
jumps in a fraction of those conditions.
He chose all of them at once.
When the plane finally landed at Reno,
federal agents swarmed it.
The aft stairs were down.
The man was gone.

The cabin held only the few
things he had left behind.
Some cigarette butts.
The black clip-on tie he had been wearing,
dropped near his seat.
And almost nothing else.
No wallet. No name.
No useful fingerprints.

A passenger who had sat among them for
hours had managed to leave less of himself

than a stranger passing
through a hotel lobby.
On the ground, the response was enormous.

Once the plane was down and
the man confirmed gone,

finding where he had landed became
something close to a military operation.

Soldiers, federal agents, and
local crews worked the rugged

country beneath the flight path
for weeks, and then for months.
Helicopters overhead.
Lines of men on foot through the timber.
They turned up nothing at all.

No parachute, no footprint,
no scrap of the cash.
Part of the problem was the land itself.

The country below that flight path
is punishing even in daylight.
Dense old-growth forest, steep ravines,

cold fast rivers, the kind of terrain
that can hide a crashed airplane,
let alone a single man.

If he came down hurt, or
came down in the water,

there were a hundred different ways for
the wilderness to take him and never give
him back.

There was also a darker detail
buried in the equipment.

One of the parachutes the authorities
handed him turned out to be a training
rig, sewn shut, useless for a real jump.

Nobody knows for certain which
chute he strapped on in the dark,
or whether the one he chose ever opened.

It is entirely possible that the most
famous skyjacker in history was dead

within minutes of stepping
off those stairs,
and that the forest simply kept the proof.

This is the moment the
case becomes the case,

because the jump has only
two possible endings,

and both of them are
unbearable in their own way.
Either he died that night.
He hit the trees at speed in the dark,

or the cold finished him, or he came
down in a river and was swept away,

and his body and his money sank into
a wilderness so vast that searchers,
even knowing roughly where to look,
never turned up a trace.
For years, teams combed that ground.
They found no parachute.
No equipment. No remains.

Not a single one of those
marked twenty-dollar bills.

Or he lived. He came
down through the storm,
gathered up his chute and his cash,
walked out of those woods before dawn,
and quietly returned to an ordinary life.
A neighbor. A coworker.

A man at the end of a bar, carrying
the secret of a perfect crime

for the rest of his days while the whole
country argued about who he might be.

Fifty years of investigation has
never been able to clearly favor

one ending over the other. And that
gap, that permanent uncertainty,

is exactly what turned
a hijacker into a folk legend.

A criminal we can picture
dying alone in the rain,

or beating the entire
system and getting away clean.
The country has never been able to choose,
so it kept both.

The FBI put a code name on
the case almost immediately.
NORJAK, short for Northwest hijacking.

What followed became one of
the longest and strangest
investigations in the Bureau's history.
In the first five years alone,

agents seriously examined more
than eight hundred suspects.
They ran down thousands of tips.

They pulled in skydivers
and ex-paratroopers,
men with grudges and men with records,

anyone who fit the loose
outline of a calm,

middle-aged man who knew
his way around a parachute.

One by one, the names were
checked and crossed off.

It is worth remembering
exactly when this happened.
1971. There was no DNA testing to fall

back on. No security
cameras watching the gate,
no body scanners, no database of faces,
no digital trail of any kind.
A passenger could pay in cash,

give a false name, sit
quietly for a few hours,

and walk away having left behind almost
nothing but a memory and a discarded tie.

The tools that crack a modern case
in days simply did not exist yet,

and by the time some of
them finally arrived,

the trail had already
gone cold by decades.

And the harder they looked,
the clearer one cruel fact became.

The man had been
clever in a very specific,
very modern way.
He had given them almost nothing to work

with. The description was generic,
a suit and a tie and dark sunglasses.
There was no usable fingerprint.

There was no photograph,
because in 1971 there was

no camera pointed at a
man in seat eighteen-E.

All the FBI ever really had was a
composite sketch built from the frightened
memories of strangers.
And a sketch is not a face.

It is a guess that everyone
agrees to treat as a face.

So the search widened, and into that gap
rushed the suspects people still argue
about today. Over the decades,

a long parade of names has been
put forward as the real D.B.

Cooper. A skydiver who pulled a strikingly
similar hijacking just months later.
A former airline employee.
An ex-soldier or two.
Men named by their own relatives,
sometimes on a deathbed.

Men named by amateur investigators
working a wall of string and photographs

in a spare bedroom. Men named by
authors with a theory and a book to sell.

A few of those names carried
real weight behind them.

Only months after Cooper, a man named
Richard McCoy pulled off a strikingly

similar hijacking, demanding
cash and parachutes and leaping

from the back of a jet in flight.
McCoy was caught for his own crime,

and for years he sat near the very top of
the list of men who might also have been

Cooper. The FBI examined him
closely and ruled him out,

concluding he simply did not match
the descriptions from Flight 305.
He is this whole case in miniature.
A vivid suspect, a satisfying story,

and then the evidence quietly
refusing to close the gap.

Other names were offered up by
the people closest to them.

A widow who said her husband
confessed on his deathbed.

A niece who recognized something
in an old family photograph.
A brother, a friend, a former coworker,

each one certain, each holding a piece
that almost fit and never quite did.

Whole books and documentaries have
been built around a single candidate.

Not one of them has ever crossed the line
from a confident story into actual proof.
Here is the part that matters most,

and the part that most
retellings quietly skip.

The FBI never confirmed
a single one of them.

Not one. Every name you have
ever heard attached to this

case was put there by someone
other than the Bureau itself.

Some of those proposed
suspects are long dead.
The status of others is murkier.
And a theory, however confident,

however slickly presented
on a late-night special,
is not a verdict.
No court has ever named D.B.
Cooper. No agency has ever named D.B.

Cooper. After everything, the chair at
the center of this story is still empty.

Over the years, the hunt curdled
into a kind of national hobby,
and it never really stopped.
Retired engineers, amateur investigators,

armchair detectives, and entire
conventions of enthusiasts have spent

decades picking over every
fragment of the case.

When investigators lifted microscopic
particles off that abandoned clip-on tie,

the hobbyists ran with it,
arguing that traces of rare metals

pointed to a man who had once
worked in aerospace or heavy industry.

Every few years a fresh team steps
forward to announce it has finally solved

the thing. Every few years, closer
scrutiny lets the air right back out.
The search has now outlasted careers,

marriages, and the lifetimes of many
of the people who first took it up.

The case did leave one
permanent mark on the world,

though, and you have benefited
from it without ever knowing.

After Cooper, and after a short rash
of copycats who tried the same trick,

the government required a simple
device on airliners with rear stairways.

A small hinged vane,
mounted by the airstair,

that the rushing air of
flight pushes into place,

locking the stairs shut so they cannot
be lowered while the plane is moving.
They still call it the Cooper vane.

It is named for a man whose
real name nobody knows,

and its only job is to make certain that
no one can ever again do exactly what he
did.

For nine years, that was
the shape of the case.
A vivid crime, a vanished man,

a mountain of dead-end tips, and
not one dollar of the ransom ever

surfacing in a bank or a shop or
a casino, anywhere in the world.

The money was as gone
as the man who took it.

And then, on a riverbank, a little
boy reached into the sand.

In 1980, a family stopped for a cookout
on the bank of the Columbia River,
at a sandy stretch called Tena Bar.

A boy about eight years
old, named Brian Ingram,

was smoothing out a patch
of sand to build a fire.

Just beneath the surface, his fingers
closed on something that was not sand.
It was paper.

It was money. Decaying,
water-rotted twenty-dollar bills,
still grouped in rubber-banded bundles,
about fifty-eight hundred dollars in all.

The FBI checked the serial
numbers against the list

they had kept for nearly
a decade. They matched.
After nine years of total silence,

a piece of D.B. Cooper's ransom
had come back into the world,

out of a riverbank, in the hands of a
child who had not been born when the crime
took place.

And here is the cruel joke
at the center of this case.

That discovery, the single
hardest piece of physical

evidence in fifty years of searching,
did not solve anything.
If anything, it deepened the mystery.

Because no one has ever been able to
fully explain how the money got there.

The spot was a long way from where
investigators believed Cooper had jumped.
The bills were buried in a way,

and worn down in a way, that experts
have been arguing about ever since.

Did the river slowly carry the cash there
over the years and bury it in the sand?
Did Cooper come down near the water,
alive, and stash it himself?

Did he die upstream and let
the current do the rest?

Every answer you reach for
creates a brand-new problem.

The one solid clue the case
ever produced points,

infuriatingly, in several
directions at once.
Then there was the tie.
That black clip-on, left on the plane,
sat in an evidence file for decades.

As forensic science advanced,
investigators went back to it and lifted
microscopic particles from its fibers,
and later a partial DNA profile.

For a moment it felt as though modern
science might finally finish what fifty
years of detective work could not.

It didn't. The particles fueled fresh
theories about where the man might have

worked, in industry,
around certain rare metals.
The DNA matched no one anyone could prove.

Like the money and the sketch
and the whole maddening case,

the tie offered just
enough to keep hope alive,
and never enough to close the file.

And the money only deepened
the puzzle in a second way.

The bills at Tena Bar came to about
fifty-eight hundred dollars.

That leaves the overwhelming
majority of the ransom,

well over a hundred and
ninety thousand dollars,
completely unaccounted for.
Out of ten thousand marked twenties,
not one other note has ever surfaced.

Not in a bank, not in a
shop, not in circulation,

not in an evidence locker
anywhere in the world.

If he lived and spent it, he did
so without ever once tripping a serial

number. If he died, the rest of it
rotted into the ground with him.

The few bills they did find became
their own small battlefield.

Some experts argued the river
had carried the cash downstream

over the years and buried it in
the sand long after the jump.

Others insisted the way the money was
layered and worn pointed to it being

placed there on purpose,
which would mean someone,

possibly Cooper himself, was
alive and moving near that riverbank.

The single hardest clue in the entire
case did not narrow the possibilities.
It multiplied them.

By 2016, the FBI had carried
NORJAK for forty-five years.

And that year, quietly,
it made a decision.
It suspended the active investigation.

Listen to that word, because
the Bureau chose it with care.
Suspended. Not solved.

To actually solve a case,
the FBI explained,

you have to be able to prove who
did it beyond a reasonable doubt,
and after four and a half decades,
none of the tips, none of the suspects,

none of the new technology
had ever delivered that proof.

So the agents who had given
pieces of their careers to this

thing set it down at last and
turned to cases they could close.
The file, sixty-six volumes thick,
was boxed and preserved.

The answer to the only question that
ever mattered was not inside it.

So we are left standing exactly
where that flight crew stood,

staring at a little warning light that
says the back of the airplane is open,

and at a space in the cabin
where a man used to be.
It is worth asking why this

one, out of all the
crimes that go unsolved,
grew into a legend.

People did not write songs about
him because he hurt someone.

He didn't. The uncomfortable truth is that
a large part of the country half wanted
him to have made it.

A polite man in a business
suit who outsmarted the airline,
the FBI, and the weather itself,

took the money, and melted into the rain
like something out of a tall tale.
If he died in those woods, it is a small,

lonely tragedy. If he lived, he pulled off
the only perfect crime America ever got
to watch unfold in real time.

And maybe that is the real reason
the case refuses to let go of us.
We are built to need endings.
The confession. The verdict.
The body. The name.

This story declines to hand
us a single one of them.
It just leaves the door open, the cold air

pouring in, and a question with no
floor underneath it. Who was he.

There is something almost unbearable
about a story that refuses to end.

We have built whole institutions
on the opposite promise.
That the truth comes out.

That patience and evidence
and science eventually win.

That no one simply steps out of a moving
airplane and out of history in the same

motion. D.B. Cooper
looked at all of that and did

exactly that, and half a century of effort
has never been able to take it back.

After fifty years, more
than eight hundred suspects,

a boy on a riverbank, and
the full weight of the FBI,

the most honest sentence
anyone can say about D.B.

Cooper is also the least
satisfying one imaginable.
We still do not know.
And we may never.
So here is where you come

in. If you have a theory,
I want to hear it.
Did he walk out of those woods,
or did the forest keep him?
Put your verdict in the comments,

and hit like if you believe a case like
this should never have been allowed to go
cold. It is the closest thing D.B.
Cooper has ever had to a jury.

And subscribe, because next
time we open another
file the world was never able to close.
